description: We are Bangladeshi undergraduate students from Computer Science, Environmental Science, Data Science, and related fields. For NASA Space Apps, we aim to explore real-world challenges, go beyond the surface, and build practical solutions using NASA’s data, technology, and resources. We welcome curious learners, researchers, problem-solvers, and builders. Let’s explore, learn, implement, and grow together.
summary:
Under the Canopy is an interactive web app that uses NISAR's L-band radar to show surface changes that cameras and most other radars miss. Its main focus is floodwater hidden under forest. NISAR's 24 cm wave reaches through leaves, clouds, smoke, and darkness. Our open Python pipeline reads NISAR GCOV HH/HV data and labels each pixel as open water or flooded vegetation, pass-by-pass, at wetland sites around the world, from Bangladesh's Sylhet hars to the Amazon, the Congo, and the Everglades. At Sylhet it found 26 km² of water under the trees, 11 km² of which Sentinel-1 C-band missed. The app also maps forest burned beneath smoke (Ontario's Thunder Bay 36 fire), ground that moved in Venezuela's M7.5 earthquake, sinking ground in Mexico City, and the flow of glaciers.

Each result is checked against independent data: river gauges, OPERA optical water maps, and GNSS stations. WorldPop then estimates how many people live within 1 km of the hidden water. The app works in English, Bangla, and Portuguese and comes with a Colab tutorial notebook. Relief teams, local communities, scientists, and students can all use it to see floods that current flood maps leave out.
details:
1. What it does

Under the Canopy is an open, interactive web app built on data from the NASA-ISRO NISAR mission. It tracks, explains, and checks four kinds of surface change. Each one is a change that NISAR's L-band radar (24 cm wavelength) can see and cameras or shorter-wavelength radar mostly cannot:

  1. Water under the trees (main focus): flood water hidden beneath forest canopy in wetlands and floodplains.
  2. Burned forest through the smoke: where wildfire removed the canopy, mapped pass by pass.
  3. Ground that moved: earthquake displacement (Venezuela, M7.2 and M7.5, 24 June 2026) and ground sinking (Mexico City), from NISAR interferograms.
  4. Ice that flows: an atlas of 28 glaciers, with NISAR's ice measurements tested against NASA's ITS_LIVE speeds.

The app currently publishes 29 detailed site maps out of 52 configured sites. These include Sylhet haor and Ratargul swamp forest (Bangladesh), the Sundarbans, the Atchafalaya Basin, the Everglades, Lago Janauacá, Mamirauá and Pacaya-Samiria (Amazon), the Pantanal, Tonlé Sap, the Okavango Delta, the Cuvette Centrale (Congo), a Limpopo flood replay in Mozambique, automatically chosen flooded-forest hotspots in Brazil, Peru, Indonesia, the Congo, Papua New Guinea and Malaysia, and wildfire sites in Canada, the USA, France, Spain, Greece, and Indonesia. Beyond these sites, a global 0.25° grid covers the rest of the planet, and 35 cells of the tropical flooded-forest "belt" have their own NISAR maps.

2. How it works

a) The science pipeline (Python)

  • Data in: It reads NISAR L2 GCOV backscatter (HH/HV), L2 GUNW interferograms, and L3 soil moisture from the Alaska Satellite Facility DAAC through Earthdata Login. It only fetches the parts of each file that cover a site, so the data stays small.
  • Flood classification: Each pixel on each pass is labelled by published radar physics. Smooth open water looks dark to the radar. Flooded forest looks very bright in HH because of the double bounce: the radar signal reflects off the water surface, then off tree trunks, and back to the satellite. A vegetation check (ESA WorldCover) and a terrain check (NASADEM, GEDI, HAND) remove false positives. The pipeline then produces area per pass, hydroperiod (days flooded in the season), and the water that C-band radar missed, measured against OPERA DSWx-S1.
  • Calibration: Thresholds are tuned per site using labels from independent maps (NASA LBA-ECO for the Amazon, the USFWS National Wetlands Inventory, OpenStreetMap swamp polygons). Scoring uses a checkerboard spatial hold-out, so a neighboring pixel can never appear in both training and test. A tuned threshold is rejected if it makes agreement with the river gauge worse. The site files record each rejection and the reason for it.
  • Burned forest: When a forest burns, HH minus HV goes up because the volume echo from the canopy disappears. Results are compared with NASA MODIS MCD64A1 and VIIRS VNP64A1 burned area. VIIRS 375 m active-fire detections date what happened between radar passes.
  • Ground motion: It unwraps the interferometric phase, removes the ionosphere, and masks pixels by coherence. Where ascending and descending passes overlap, it splits the motion into east and vertical parts. For subsidence it fits a time series. For the earthquake, it forward-models the USGS finite-fault model with Okada (1985) and compares the result with our map. Our Okada code reproduces Okada's published test case to four digits.
  • Glaciers: It combines ITS_LIVE speed, trend, and seasonal swing (1985–2024), traces flowlines to draw time-distance diagrams, adds GRACE/GRACE-FO regional mass, and records which NISAR passes cover each glacier.
  • People: WorldPop population, OpenStreetMap roads and places, and GeoNames villages answer the question of who lives within 1 km of the hidden water and which roads are under it.
  • Outlook (experimental): It fits the hidden flood on each pass against the main river's flow (GEOGloWS ECMWF), then follows that river's 15-day forecast. It never goes beyond the range of flows seen during the season.
  • Output: All results are written to a fixed, versioned data format (JSON schemas, binary pixel grids, PNGs, GeoJSON, CSV). The web app reads nothing else.

b) The web app (plain JavaScript, zero runtime dependencies)
The app is a static site hosted on GitHub Pages. It loads no frameworks, needs no account or API key, and keeps working offline once loaded. The browser classifier (rules.js) is an exact port of the Python classifier, and an automated test checks that both give identical results.

3. Features, what each one does, and who it is for

Exploring the map (everyone)

  • Mode switch: Water, Fire, Ground and Ice, all with the same layout and controls.
  • Timeline and play: steps through every 12-day NISAR pass of the season.
  • Hidden-flood reveal: a swipe from photo to C-band radar to NISAR. At Sylhet the photo is 99% cloud, and NISAR finds water that C-band missed.
  • Map layers: per-pass classes, days flooded, water-level change under the canopy (from interferograms), GEDI canopy height and cover, and NASA basemaps (Blue Marble, Black Marble).
  • Explain this pixel: gives a plain-language verdict for a spot, the radar numbers behind it, and that spot's history over the season.
  • Map notes: marks the main feature in each view with its value, unit and date, following cartographic labelling rules.
  • Anywhere on Earth / What's here: click any place to see what NASA's global products say about that 0.25° cell (NISAR coverage, forest, wetland, CYGNSS water, GRACE groundwater, population), and jump to the nearest detailed site.
  • NASA live layers (GIBS): daily global imagery for any date. Active fires: VIIRS and MODIS fire detections worldwide, colored by fire radiative power. Floods reported now: current GDACS flood events.
  • Satellite tracks and next pass: shows the NISAR orbit that imaged each pass, its look angle, the predicted next pass, and the day/night line.

Disaster and relief teams (humanitarian groups, civil defense, NGOs)

  • Village flood card: one printable, phone-friendly image per pass. It shows the settlements next to hidden water, how many days each was flooded, roads under water, people within 1 km, and when NISAR passes next. It is available in Bengali for Sylhet and works offline. At Sylhet's peak, about 318,000 people live within 1 km of the hidden flood, and about 334 km of roads are flooded.
  • Honest timing: each card states that it is for planning relief, not a flash-flood warning, because NISAR products arrive days after a pass.

Communities and local offices

  • The full interface, the flood card, and the game are in English, Bengali, and Portuguese (2,072 translated strings in each language).
  • Label mode: residents mark places they know flooded. These marks are used as independent checks on the map, never as hidden training data.
  • Place a search and a per-spot count of days flooded.

Radar and water scientists

  • Scientist mode: move any threshold, and the map recomputes in the browser, giving exactly the same result as the pipeline.
  • Radar feature space: a scatter plot of every pixel (HH against HH−HV) with the decision boundaries drawn on it. Drag a box to highlight those pixels on the map.
  • Ridge plot: the flood pulse shown directly in the radar values, one distribution per pass.
  • Change statistics: an omnibus likelihood-ratio change test (Conradsen et al. 2016), a Mann–Kendall trend test with an exact p-value plus the Theil–Sen slope, and patch tracking that follows each flooded patch as it appears, grows, merges, splits, or disappears.
  • Where the water went: an alluvial diagram of pixel-class flows from the first pass to the peak to the last pass.
  • Analyst tools: measure distance and area, statistics inside a drawn area, cross-sections, and UTM and lat/lon readouts.
  • Ground-motion tools: color maps that stay readable with color vision deficiency (Crameri), fringes, profiles with the median and interquartile range against the USGS model, GNSS time series at stations, and a second-by-second rupture animation built from the fault model.
  • Open data: GeoTIFF (written in the browser), GeoJSON, and CSV for every pass, plus a shareable link that reopens the exact view.
  • Analyze here: when the app is run locally, it builds a new detailed site for any place you pick.

Climate and methane modellers

  • Methane ledger: hidden-flood area × days flooded × methane emission rates published for flooded forests. It is shown as a range, never as a single number, along with the share that C-band missed.
  • Flooded-forest belt: forest, water, GRACE storage, and WetCHARTs methane across the tropics, cell by cell.
  • What drove it: GPM IMERG rainfall, CYGNSS water, and NISAR soil moisture on the same timeline as the radar passes. Is this a wet year? : GRACE basin storage compared with 2004–2023.

Wildfire and cryosphere users

  • Burned-area charts: area burned by date, agreement with MODIS and VIIRS and how that depends on the threshold, active fires between passes, and how clear the optical view was on each pass.
  • Downwind ice: for the Columbia Icefield, fire upwind, smoke over the ice (VIIRS aerosol), and ice darkening (VIIRS albedo), all compared with earlier years. It is presented as co-occurrence, never as cause.
  • Glacier atlas: flow shown as moving particles, trends, seasonal swing, speed history from 1985 to 2024, comparison with published speeds, and GRACE mass.

Students and teachers

  • "Find the hidden water" game: players guess where water lies under the trees on real NISAR maps, then NISAR reveals the answer next to what C-band saw.
  • 59 Google Colab notebooks (one per site, event, and glacier) with the real data embedded: one click, nothing to install. The main tutorial goes from radar physics to classification, L-band against C-band, river-gauge checks, threshold sensitivity, a machine-learning comparison (scikit-learn/PyTorch), taking results into GIS, and the method's limits.
  • "How we know" field guide: four chapters (water, fire, ground, ice), each in five steps: the question, the physics (drawn), the rule, how it was checked, and where it can be wrong.
  • Guided story mode, an opening film, sonification (hear the flood pulse), and Earth's waltz: each season played in 3/4 time with one bar per NISAR pass, where a clashing note marks the water C-band missed. The waltz also produces a downloadable poster.

Planners, funders and press

  • Four types of change explained with one method, an evidence-first landing page, a "what we do not claim" section, a sources page listing every dataset with its licence and citation, and print-ready cards in three languages.

4. How we check the results

Every result is checked against data that was not used to tune it:

  • Sylhet: NISAR flood area against the Surma river gauge (BWDB). Correlation r = 0.94 over 7 passes, and 0.98 with the best time lag.
  • Thunder Bay 36: NISAR burned area against NASA MODIS.
  • Venezuela: our map against JPL's own processing and the USGS fault model, including radar geometries the USGS did not use.
  • Mexico City: sinking rate against Nevada Geodetic Laboratory GNSS stations.

Known limits are stated openly in the app:

  • Burned forest can look like flooded forest to the radar, and the map flags this.
  • Near Caracas airport our earthquake map and the USGS model differ by about 41 cm, and the app shows both.
  • NISAR data is a provisional release.
  • Demo data is always badged SYNTHETIC.

5. Benefits and intended impact

  • Closing a blind spot: flooded forest is missing from most flood maps, yet it is where many rural communities live (Sylhet, the Amazon várzea, the Congo). NISAR makes it visible, and Under the Canopy turns that into maps people can act on, in their own language.
  • Relief planning by village, road and population.
  • Better climate inputs: how long forested wetlands stay flooded is one of the least certain inputs to the global methane budget.
  • Education and trust: open code (Apache-2.0), open data, visible uncertainty, and every number traceable to a file.
  • Scalable at no cost: the global belt is built with free NASA data on GitHub Actions. The app runs on a modest laptop, so a district office can use it.

6. Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: Python (pipeline), JavaScript (ES modules, no framework), HTML/CSS, Jupyter notebooks.
  • Python libraries: NumPy (the core pipeline uses only NumPy, with its own UTM projection and PNG encoder), h5py, rasterio/GDAL, earthaccess, asf_search, scikit-learn and PyTorch (notebooks), matplotlib.
  • Web: hand-written map renderer, Mapbox Vector Tile decoder, GeoTIFF writer, canvas and SVG charts, Web Audio, i18n.
  • Testing and CI: pytest and ruff, Node's built-in test runner, Playwright end-to-end tests, and GitHub Actions (CI, the Pages deploy, and a parallel workflow that builds the belt).
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages. Notebooks are on Google Colab and Google Drive. A local Python server runs "Analyse here".
  • Data (all credited on the sources page): NISAR GCOV/GUNW/soil moisture, OPERA DSWx/RTC, HLS, NASADEM, GEDI, SWOT, GRACE/GRACE-FO, GPM IMERG, CYGNSS, SMAP, ICESat-2, MODIS, VIIRS, ITS_LIVE, WetCHARTs, SEDAC, GIBS, plus USGS, ANA, BWDB, GDACS, NGL GNSS, RGI, ESA WorldCover, JRC Global Surface Water, GLWD, GEOGloWS, WorldPop, GeoNames and OpenStreetMap.
  • Hardware: standard laptops. No special hardware or paid cloud services.

7. What makes it creative

  • It picked only the changes that need L-band, so NISAR is the reason the app exists rather than an extra layer.
  • Learning by missing it: the game and the photo, C-band and NISAR reveal let people fail to see the water first, then show them what the radar found.
  • Earth's waltz: the challenge's metaphor taken literally, with NISAR's 12-day repeat as the beat and the season played as music.
  • The village flood card turns a radar product into something a union council can print.
  • The methane ledger links hidden water to the global methane budget.
  • The earthquake rupture animation plays the fault model second by second, then shows NISAR's measured result.
  • The analysis runs in the browser, giving the same result as the pipeline, so anyone can question the thresholds.

8. What we considered

  • Scientific honesty: independent checks, rejected calibrations, uncertainty bands, synthetic data always flagged, and no alerts or forecasts presented as warnings.
  • Accessibility: colour maps safe for colour-vision deficiency, a text version of the film, readable cards, mobile layouts, and three languages (translations are marked as drafts until native speakers review them).
  • Low-resource users: works offline, no accounts, small files, runs on modest hardware.
  • Licensing and attribution: every source is cited with its licence, and the code is Apache-2.0.
  • Privacy and security: Earthdata credentials stay on the user's machine, and the browser makes no API calls except for map tiles.
  • Reproducibility: fixed data formats, test coverage, CI, and notebooks that run on their own content.
